name: Transmigration and the fate of souls
plain_explanation: After death, the philosopher's purified soul goes to live in bliss with the gods, while lesser souls are reborn as animals fitting their character -- cowardly or unrighteous men become asses, wolves, or hawks, while merely virtuous non-philosophers become social insects like bees.
precise_definition: Plato's account of post-mortem judgment in which the truly philosophic soul, liberated in life from bodily 'thraldom,' departs to the invisible world to dwell with the gods, while impure souls either haunt sepulchres as ghosts or are reborn into animal bodies suited to their moral character.
why_it_mattered: It supplies the practical, ethical payoff of the whole theory: only philosophy secures the best afterlife, which is Plato's stated reason for the philosopher's ascetic self-discipline.
historical_origin: Drawn from Orphic and Pythagorean doctrines of the soul's transmigration.
examples: 'No one who has not studied philosophy and who is not entirely pure at the time of his departure is allowed to enter the company of the Gods, but the lover of knowledge only.'
connection_to_politics_or_religion: Directly continuous with Orphic religious eschatology.
